newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SIMEX fuel oil future resurrection seen short-lived.
newsitem.headline: SIMEX fuel oil future resurrection seen short-lived.

text.p: The revival of the SIMEX fuel oil futures contract this week could be short-lived unless changes are made, traders said.
The Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) had urged the oil industry to resume trading the futures contract as a sign of goodwill.
The authority is considering changes to the contract, which had been dormant since August last year when traders withdrew because of a lack of liquidity in the market.

But since Monday, only 42 lots -- or just 42,000 tonnes -- have been traded that brokers said would not be sufficient to keep the contract going. At least several hundred lots needed to be traded each day for the contract to survive, they said.
"Performance so far has been terrible, and it will probably die a natural death again due to lack of activity," a fuel oil trader said.
Traders said the specifications of the contract were out of line with the cash market, making them reluctant to trade.
There was also uncertainty over possible changes to the contract, they said. Market participants did not want to have oustanding positions if changes were made.
"Traders who currently hold position on the contract may be forced to take (physical) delivery when the contract expires if illiquidity persists," said a broker.
The existing contract is based on 4.0 percent sulphur fuel oil. But the underlying cash market focuses on 3.5 percent sulphur fuel oil.

The contract allows sellers to nominate a wide loading range for fuel oil deliveries against the contract between the fifth and 25th working day each month, which critics say is not economical for buyers.
"Most traders are still very unwilling to trade the contract as some of the specifications on the contracts were not changed," a broker told Reuters.
A SIMEX source said the exchange "has provided the tool but it cannot make commercial decisions for traders".
"While the volumes on SIMEX were lower than expected, traders have to make up their own mind whether they want or need such a tool...if they want a futures contract they have to nurture it," he said.
SIMEX proposed changes in the contract to the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) in July. The authority has yet to grant approval.

The proposed changes include reducing the sulphur content and narrowing the loading-date window for physical deliveries to between the 11th and 20th business day of the month. Also, to allow players to take physical delivery in multiples of 10,000 tonnes instead of the existing 1,000-tonne-lots.
Decisions over deliveries and dates would also be more equally negotiated between buyers and sellers. The current contract specifications favoured the sellers, some trader said.
The SIMEX high sulphur fuel oil contract was launched in February 1989.
